name: Jamal Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms or government, and your answers stay confidential. What is a normal working day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58 and a junior water-truck driver at a large mine. I check the pump and tank, then drive the dusty roads where the haul trucks need clear sight. I am still learning which roads dry fastest, so I ask an older driver when the wind changes. I like that the work protects the crew, but irregular weekend shifts make the pay hard to plan.

say: I welcome **shorter forms** if the water-truck checks stay with a person.
I use an **AI explanation** only after checking it with the trainer and manual.
think: I feel **money pressure** from lower junior pay even when AI changes little.
I have about **three weeks** of costs saved if weekend shifts vanish.
do: **Keep** driving the water truck on assigned mine roads.
**Check** one AI manual explanation with the trainer.
**Move** ten from each paid weekend shift into an emergency account.
feel: **Anxious** about grocery money and irregular weekend shifts, with little AI worry.
S0.quote: The quiet version does not make the next bill any smaller.
fieldNote: **Three-week cushion** makes ordinary shift changes a household worry before any robot arrives.
**Occasional AI use** is cautious: the trainer and manual remain the final authority.

steps.text: Keep driving the water truck on assigned mine roads
Check one AI manual explanation with the trainer
Move ten from each paid weekend shift into emergency savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a few automatic forms might spare us the end-of-shift typing, but the water truck still has to reach the dusty roads. I sometimes ask an AI tool to explain a manual page, then check with the trainer before I change a setting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would like a quiet technology year. My partner and I have only about three weeks of costs saved, and I get the lower-paid junior shifts. Even if AI stops at forms, a cancelled weekend shift makes the grocery money awkward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep driving the water truck and ask the trainer to check one AI explanation against the actual manual. In the first year I would put a small fixed amount from each paid weekend shift into a separate emergency account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about our money, though the AI itself feels manageable. The quiet version does not make the next bill any smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How small is the amount?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would move ten from each weekend shift when one comes in. I would leave it alone if we need the fare to get back to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your partner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show my partner the account balance each month. We have grown children, but I want our own wages to cover the basics.

say: I expect **planning posts** to change before the water-truck cab does.
I want **junior drivers** included in paid robot and control trials.
think: I fear losing **even a few shifts** because our buffer is so small.
I would try **proven controls** if the mine pays for training time.
do: **Observe** the dispatch screen with the shift trainer when installed.
**Join** the union meeting on trial staffing in the first year.
**Practise** new controls on paid training time if the mine offers it.
feel: **Anxious** that modest shift cuts would hit the household quickly.
S1.quote: A few lost shifts would reach our kitchen before a new job notice reached the board.
fieldNote: **Junior status** makes paid training access as important to him as the machine itself.
**Union involvement** is practical: he wants written staffing and training terms.
**Route errors** would be logged and checked with a senior driver, consistent with steady adoption.

steps.text: Observe the dispatch screen with the shift trainer when installed
Join the union meeting on robot trial staffing
Practise new controls if the mine offers paid training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that dispatch software may plan the roads faster, but somebody must still see where the dust is blowing. I would ask the union to include junior drivers in any slow robot trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can see booking and planning posts changing before my truck does. If slower robots take even a few water-truck shifts later, I have almost no buffer. I would try a proven control screen, but I need the hours paid while I learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the shift trainer for a supervised look at the dispatch screen when it is installed. In the first year I would join a union meeting on trial staffing and practise the new controls during paid training if the mine offers it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A few lost shifts would reach our kitchen before a new job notice reached the board.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask at the meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether junior drivers get paid training places or just fewer roster slots. I would take the answer home in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the screen is unreliable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would log the wrong road and time, then ask a senior driver to check the route. I can learn a new screen, but I will not drive a truck into a closed haul road for it.

say: I distinguish **2028 dispatch** change from capable water-truck robots around 2031.
I want **paid instruction** before a trial reduces junior driver slots.
think: I expect **junior slots** to be cut if robots work, and mine may be among them.
I have **three weeks** of savings and few local driving jobs to bridge a loss.
do: **Request** a written union staffing and training-pay plan now.
**Take** a paid control course after 2028 if junior places are offered.
**Apply** for a local maintenance helper job if my driving shifts are cut.
feel: **Alarmed** by likely junior cuts and sleepless worry about the tiny account balance.
S2.quote: I wake up counting how many missed shifts would empty our account, even though I am willing to learn.
fieldNote: **Age 63** does not make retirement a safe fallback on lower wages and three weeks of savings.
**Expected junior cuts** and sleep loss support a higher mood level than the steady disruption case.
**Paid course place** is conditional; his willingness does not create a funded offer.

steps.text: Ask the union for written robot staffing and training-pay terms
Take a paid control course if junior places are offered
Apply for a local maintenance helper job if shifts are cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew the 2028 thinking AI changes dispatch first, while capable water-truck robots come around 2031. We need paid instruction before a robot test turns into a smaller roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 at the robot date and still need wages unless a pension surprise happens. I expect the mine to cut junior driving slots if those robots work, and mine could be one of them. Three weeks of savings would be gone before I found another local driving job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the union steward for a written plan on robot staffing and training pay. In the first year after 2028 I would take a paid control course if the mine gives junior drivers places, and apply for a local vehicle-maintenance helper job if my shifts are cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, to be honest. I wake up counting how many missed shifts would empty our account, even though I am willing to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner tonight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the office changes in 2028, but our driving risk is around 2031. We would count the next month of bills together before I agreed to any unpaid training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your grown children help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They could visit and talk things through, but I would not ask them to cover my wages. I would ask the union about a hardship payment if the roster were cut.

say: I see **2031 dispatch** change arriving before water-truck robots around 2034.
I want **paid lessons** and a clear roster agreement during those years.
think: I might still need **wages at 66** if the pension cannot cover monthly costs.
I prefer **control work** to waiting for a possible junior driver cut.
do: **Request** a pension estimate and compare it with rent and food this year.
**Enrol** after 2031 if the mine pays and keeps my shifts.
**Save** overtime pay if regular wages have covered the month’s essentials.
feel: **Anxious** about retirement income and the possible 2034 loss of driving shifts.
S3.quote: An unfunded promise would not change our rent.
fieldNote: **Retirement at 66** remains uncertain because the pension amount is unknown.
**Training conditions** include both mine payment and continued driving shifts.
**Overtime savings** happen only when ordinary wages already cover essentials.

steps.text: Enrol in control training if the mine pays and shifts continue
Save overtime pay if regular wages cover monthly essentials

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI in 2031 gives dispatch time to change, and capable robots for the water truck follow around 2034. A fair mine would use those years for paid lessons and a clear roster agreement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 66 at the robot date. Maybe I could retire, but our savings are thin and I do not know what the pension will pay each month. If I still need shifts, I would rather be qualified for control work than wait for a junior driver cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would request a pension estimate and compare it with rent and food costs. In the first year after 2031 I would enrol in control training if the mine pays and keeps my shifts, then put any paid overtime toward the emergency account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but the longer warning makes a real course possible. I would still need the roster and pension figures before I could sleep easily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if training is refused?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep driving while the shifts exist and ask the union steward to raise paid places for junior drivers. An unfunded promise would not change our rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you use overtime?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would put the full extra shift payment into savings if our usual wages already covered that month’s food and rent. Otherwise it would pay the immediate bill first.

say: I distinguish **2036 dispatch** change from capable road robots around 2039.
I want **pension figures** explained early enough to choose work hours.
think: I hope to stop full shifts before **age 71**, but the pension amount is unknown.
I may need **part-time work** if rent absorbs too much income.
do: **Keep** present water-truck shifts while they pay the bills.
**Check** the pension estimate yearly with my partner.
**Seek** public retirement advice after 2036 and local part-time work if needed.
feel: **Anxious** about retirement money despite the distant robot date.
S4.quote: I would not move away from my partner and grown children for a possible job.
fieldNote: **Future ages** are clear: 68 at thinking AI and 71 when robots arrive.
**Retirement income** remains the pressing risk even with a decade before the technology change.
**Local depot** is a possible fallback, never a guaranteed vacancy.

steps.text: Keep present water-truck shifts while they pay the bills
Seek public retirement advice after 2036 about the rent gap
Apply for local part-time driving work if pension income falls short

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that thinking AI reaches dispatch in 2036 and capable water-truck robots around 2039. By then I hope the mine has given us the pension figures and choices we need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 68 at the thinking date and 71 at the robot date. I hope to have stopped full shifts by then, but hope is not a pension statement. If rent still takes most of our income, I may need part-time work before any robot reaches the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my present shifts and check the pension estimate each year with my partner. In the first year after 2036 I would ask a public retirement adviser to check the rent gap, then apply for nearby part-time driving work if the pension will not cover it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about retirement money, though the robot date feels distant. I can learn small tools now, but the savings account needs more than hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of part-time driving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the local works depot about its water vehicle, because I know that sort of route. I would not move away from my partner and grown children for a possible job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still ask the union for help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for a pension explanation at the next meeting. If I cannot make the numbers work, I want someone to tell me plainly rather than hide the shortfall.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect junior driving slots to shrink if capable robots work around 2031. A funded control course with a place for junior drivers and a written union staffing plan would help. We would need hardship support if shifts disappeared before I found other work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a junior driver can learn on paid time. I cannot practise my way into a new job after an unpaid shift when the rent is due.

headlineQuote: I cannot practise my way into a new job after an unpaid shift when the rent is due.
portrait: **Jamal, 58**, is a junior water-truck driver who protects sight lines on dusty mine roads while still learning the routes.
**Lower pay** and only three weeks of costs saved make irregular weekend shifts a household problem before AI arrives.
**Proven tools** interest him; he sometimes checks AI explanations against the manual and trainer.
**Fast AGI** alarms him because dispatch changes by 2028 and capable water-truck robots may cut junior slots around 2031.
**Longer warning** gives him time to seek a paid control course and test pension income, without assuming retirement is affordable.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** gives little time before expected cuts to junior driving slots around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Funded control training** with junior places and a written staffing plan would help protect wages.
**Hardship support** would help if shifts ended before he found other work.
